problem: EQA agents are almost always evaluated episodically, with memory reset after every question. It is therefore unknown whether their memory architectures (2D occupancy maps, pose-tagged semantic libraries, 3D reconstructions, implicit VLA hidden states) can actually accumulate and reuse knowledge across several questions asked in the same scene. The common assumption that leaving memory 'on' uniformly helps has not been tested.
motivation: Real robots operate continuously, and re-exploring from scratch for every query is prohibitively inefficient. The paper observes that simply carrying memory forward across queries mostly shortens navigation without improving answers. Geometric maps remember where the agent went but not what it saw. VLAs trained on short episodes treat long multi-query histories as out-of-distribution input. Independent pose-tagged memory entries add retrieval noise as history grows.
key_idea: Sequentialize an existing EQA benchmark (OpenEQA) by chaining all questions of a scene while carrying agent memory forward with frozen weights. Measuring the memory advantage in accuracy and in path length then diagnoses which memory architectures truly accumulate knowledge; spatially grounded 3D memory (3D-Mem) is the one that does.
insight: Memory persistence ≠ knowledge accumulation. Under the identical minimal persistence protocol, ExploreEQA (+2.7 MA, 0.0 SA), MemoryEQA (+1.4 MA, -0.5 SA) and UniNavid (+0.9 MA, -1.5 SA) gain almost nothing. Only 3D-Mem, which fuses observations onto metric 3D geometry, gains both accuracy (+33.3 MA) and efficiency (+53.3 SA), and it is the only agent with a consistently positive per-query-index accuracy Δ. Two caveats temper this. First, 3D-Mem's large MA is partly a consequence of its very weak episodic baseline (SR 25.5, PL 5.6 m, suggesting premature stopping or under-exploration). Second, its sequential SR (58.8) still does not exceed MemoryEQA's episodic SR (61.0). So the result shows reuse capability rather than best absolute accuracy.
method: Sequential-EQA protocol: questions in the same environment form an ordered sequence. Episodic runs use τ_i ~ π(q_i, m_0=∅); sequential runs use τ_{i+1} ~ π(q_{i+1}, m_i), inheriting the terminal memory of the previous query.

Benchmark sequentialization: OpenEQA questions are regrouped by scene into scene-level sequences of variable length N_k (most scenes have 10–13 questions; >60% have ≥10). Order is shuffled with a fixed seed shared by all agents and conditions; all sequences are evaluated without truncation.

Metrics: SR (episodic accuracy), SR_mem (sequential accuracy), Memory Advantage MA = SR_mem − SR, PL / PL_mem (geodesic path length without / with memory), and Step Advantage SA = (PL − PL_mem)/PL × 100%.

Minimal memory adaptation protocol: (1) state inheritance, with no truncation or summarization; (2) query update, re-initializing goal-directed planners; (3) frozen weights, with no recalibration or sequential training. Any episodic-vs-sequential difference is thus attributed to memory structure alone.

Memory-paradigm taxonomy and agents: VLM-agent with geometric memory (ExploreEQA: occupancy + VLM-scored frontiers), dense episodic semantic memory (MemoryEQA: RGB+pose+caption+embedding with entropy-based retrieval), structured 3D spatial-semantic memory (3D-Mem: point cloud + visual embeddings with spatially indexed lookup), and VLA with implicit latent memory (UniNavid).
Per-query-index analysis: accuracy and navigation time at query position i, averaged over scenes with N_k ≥ i, to test whether memory usefulness grows along the sequence.

Real-robot validation: a Unitree Go2 with a RealSense D435i and LiDAR L2 runs one episodic and one sequential 5-question trial per environment (lab, lobby, hallway; plus an outdoor rooftop for UniNavid). The robot is reset to the same start pose before each query.

setting.backbone: Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, FP8-quantized (frozen), used by the VLM-agent methods ExploreEQA, MemoryEQA and 3D-Mem. UniNavid uses its own pre-trained, fine-tuned VLA weights, kept frozen. No model is trained in this paper.
setting.training_data: none; this is an evaluation protocol. All agent weights are frozen and unchanged; UniNavid uses its original episodic training.
setting.observation: Egocentric RGB-D + pose for the VLM agents (map / 3D reconstruction building); a short window of RGB frames + language query for UniNavid. Real robot: RealSense D435i RGB-D + LiDAR.
setting.action_space: Agent-specific. Frontier / waypoint selection for the VLM agents (ExploreEQA, MemoryEQA, 3D-Mem); predicted navigation waypoints / actions for UniNavid.
setting.simulator: Simulated OpenEQA indoor scenes. The simulator is not explicitly named; qualitative figures refer to MP3D scenes.
setting.privileged: None beyond the agent's own memory inherited from earlier queries in the same scene (the manipulated variable). Agents use pose for mapping. The real robot is reset to the same start location before each query.

numbers_note: This is a diagnostic evaluation paper with no new method. All numbers are the authors' own runs of four existing agents (ExploreEQA, MemoryEQA, 3D-Mem, UniNavid) under the new Sequential-EQA protocol, so they are not comparable to those agents' originally published OpenEQA numbers. 3D-Mem is treated as the focal method. SR here is a percentage accuracy; figures report the OpenEQA 1–5 answer score, and the mapping to % is not explained. PL is defined as a total sum but its values look like per-question means. Standard errors, navigation time/distance and per-query-index results appear only in figures. The number of scenes and questions is not stated.
results: Carrying memory across queries gives near-zero accuracy gains for three of the four architectures: ExploreEQA MA +2.7 / SA 0.0, MemoryEQA +1.4 / −0.5, UniNavid +0.9 / −1.5. Only 3D-Mem's spatially grounded 3D memory improves both accuracy (SR 25.5 → 58.8, MA +33.3) and navigation cost (PL 5.6 → 2.6, SA +53.3), with sustained positive per-query accuracy Δ. MemoryEQA still has the highest absolute accuracy (61.0 / 62.4). On a real Unitree Go2, 3D-Mem rises from 20% to 40% and MemoryEQA from 40% to 47%, UniNavid stays at 15%, and ExploreEQA drops from 33% to 26%.
limitations: Agents are adapted with naive state inheritance and no tuning, so the conclusions describe failure modes under minimal persistence, not the best achievable sequential performance. Some of 3D-Mem's gain reflects a very weak episodic baseline (SR 25.5, PL 5.6 m).

Only one benchmark source (OpenEQA) and a single VLM backbone (Qwen3-VL-8B) are used, and question/scene counts are unstated. The real-robot study is tiny (≈15–20 questions per method, one trial per condition), so its differences are not statistically meaningful, as the authors themselves note for ExploreEQA.

Some reporting is inconsistent: qualitative figures show MP3D scenes, PL is defined as a total but reported like a mean, and claims such as memory becoming 'exponentially more useful' are not quantitatively supported.
